title: Mendel's Peas: Segregation and Independent Assortment

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In the modern reading of Mendel's pea crosses, how does a plant pass on a gene to its gametes?
cards.back: It carries two copies of each gene and puts one of them, chosen like a fair coin toss, into each egg or pollen grain.
cards.quote: Each pea plant carries two copies of each gene and puts one of them, chosen like a fair coin toss, into each egg or pollen grain.

cards.front: For genes that assort independently, the chance of a combination of alleles is the {{c1::product}} of the separate chances.
cards.back: Each gene gets its own coin.
cards.quote: For genes that assort independently, each gene gets its own coin, so the chance of a combination is the product of the separate chances.

cards.front: Besides random segregation, what does the coin-toss rule assume about transmission, fertilisation and survival when it predicts a pea cross?
cards.back: That transmission of the two alleles is equal, eggs and pollen meet at random, and all offspring survive equally. It predicts averages, not exact counts.
cards.quote: The rule predicts averages, not exact counts, and assumes that transmission is equal, eggs and pollen meet at random, and all offspring survive equally.

cards.front: Mendel's selfed round-by-wrinkled pea hybrids bore 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled seeds. Compute the round-to-wrinkled ratio and the wrinkled fraction.
cards.back: 5,474 / 1,850 = 2.96 round per wrinkled seed. Wrinkled fraction = 1,850 / 7,324 = 0.25, about 1 in 4, as a 3:1 predicts.
cards.quote: Gregor Mendel counted 7,324 seeds borne by his round-by-wrinkled pea hybrids: 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled.

cards.front: In pea genetics, what is a true-breeding line?
cards.back: A line kept by self-pollination whose selfed plants give offspring showing the same form, generation after generation.
cards.quote: in a true-breeding line, the offspring of selfed plants show the same form, generation after generation.

cards.front: Mendel crossed each pair of pea varieties both ways, each serving once as seed parent and once as pollen parent. What did these reciprocal crosses show?
cards.back: Both directions gave the same hybrid: it did not matter which parent was the mother.
cards.quote: These reciprocal crosses gave the same hybrid: it did not matter which parent was the mother.

cards.front: In modern labels for a pea cross, the true-breeding parents are the P generation, their hybrids the F1, and the offspring of selfed F1 plants the {{c1::F2}}.
cards.quote: the true-breeding parents are the P generation, their hybrids the F1, and the offspring of selfed F1 plants the F2.

cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene, such as R (round) or r (wrinkled) for pea seed shape.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene (a card, in the films).

cards.front: A gene's place on a chromosome is its {{c1::locus}}.
cards.back: Mendel had no idea of such a place.
cards.quote: A gene's place on a chromosome is its locus (see chromosomes and meiosis); Mendel had no idea of such a place.

cards.front: For pea seed shape, distinguish genotype from phenotype.
cards.back: Genotype is the pair of alleles a plant carries (RR, Rr or rr). Phenotype is what you can see (round or wrinkled).
cards.quote: The genotype is the pair of alleles a plant carries (RR, Rr or rr).

cards.front: A pea plant whose two alleles at the seed-shape locus are the same (RR or rr) is {{c1::homozygous}}.
cards.back: One whose alleles differ (Rr) is heterozygous.
cards.quote: Homozygous means the two alleles are the same (RR or rr).

cards.front: In a pea cross, what makes a character dominant and what makes one recessive, as Mendel used the terms?
cards.back: Dominant: seen, wholly or nearly unchanged, in the hybrid (round). Recessive: latent in the hybrid and reappears later (wrinkled).
cards.quote: wrinkled the recessive character, the one that becomes latent in the hybrid and reappears later.

cards.front: An Rr pea self-pollinates. What fraction of all its seeds is expected to be Rr, and what fraction round?
cards.back: Each box of the grid is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Rr arises two ways (R egg + r pollen, r egg + R pollen): 1/2. Round = RR + Rr = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
cards.why: One R is enough for a round seed, so three of the four boxes look round.
cards.quote: Rr x Rr → 1/4 RR : 1/2 Rr : 1/4 rr, which shows as 3/4 round : 1/4 wrinkled

cards.front: Plants are grown from the round F2 seeds of a selfed Rr pea and each is allowed to self-pollinate. What fraction should give only round seeds, and what should the rest give?
cards.back: One third should breed true (RR); two thirds (Rr) should give round and wrinkled seeds again, near 3:1. Round F2 seeds are 1 RR : 2 Rr.
cards.why: Mendel found 193 of 565 plants (34 percent) bred true and 372 segregated.
cards.quote: So one round plant in three should breed true, and two in three should give round and wrinkled seeds again.

cards.front: Why did Mendel's F3 progeny test of round F2 plants explain the 3:1 ratio rather than just repeat it?
cards.back: Round plants that look identical split 1 true-breeding to 2 segregating, showing round seeds come in two hidden kinds (RR and Rr) in the proportions the coin toss predicts.
cards.quote: The 1-to-2 split among plants that look identical says why: round seeds come in two hidden kinds, in the proportions the coin toss predicts.

cards.front: Law of segregation: the two alleles of a plant separate into {{c1::different gametes}}, one to each, at random.
cards.quote: This is the law of segregation: the two alleles of a plant separate into different gametes, one to each, at random.

cards.front: In a selfed Rr pea, which ratio is 3:1 and which is 1:2:1?
cards.back: 3:1 is the phenotype ratio (round : wrinkled, what you see). 1:2:1 is the genotype ratio (RR : Rr : rr, what the plants carry).
cards.quote: Keep two ratios apart: 3:1 is a phenotype ratio, what you see; 1:2:1 is a genotype ratio, what the plants carry.

cards.front: What does it mean, and not mean, to say an allele is dominant?
cards.back: It describes only what a heterozygote looks like. It does not mean the allele is stronger, better, or commoner in a population.
cards.quote: Dominance describes only what a heterozygote looks like. It does not mean an allele is stronger, better, or commoner in a population.

cards.front: Why do rr pea seeds wrinkle?
cards.back: r carries an insertion in a gene for a starch-branching enzyme (SBEI). rr embryos make less amylopectin and hold more sugar, take up more water as they develop, and wrinkle as they dry.
cards.quote: Without that enzyme (the SBEI form), rr embryos make less amylopectin, the branched form of starch (see carbohydrates), and hold more sugar

cards.front: What is a common reason an enzyme-gene allele like pea r is recessive?
cards.back: One working copy of the enzyme's gene makes enough enzyme, so the heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote.
cards.quote: That is a common reason an allele is recessive: one working copy of an enzyme's gene makes enough enzyme

cards.front: RR and Rr pea seeds are both round. Would you expect their starch grains to be identical? What does this say about "round is dominant"?
cards.back: Not necessarily: Rr starch grains have been reported to be intermediate between RR and rr. Dominance describes one phenotype at a time; round is dominant for seed shape, not for everything the gene does.
cards.quote: the starch grains inside Rr seeds have been reported to be intermediate between those of RR and rr seeds.

cards.front: Suppose a pea enzyme gene where one working copy is not enough for the normal phenotype, so the heterozygote looks different from both homozygotes. What phenotype ratio would a selfed heterozygote give?
cards.back: No 3:1. Three visible classes in about 1:2:1, because the phenotype now tracks the genotype ratio.
cards.why: A 3:1 needs complete dominance: one copy of each form must look like two dominant copies. Without it, the Rr boxes form their own class.
cards.quote: A 3:1 ratio also needs complete dominance: a plant with one copy of each form looks just like one with two dominant copies.

cards.front: One selfed round-by-wrinkled pea hybrid bore 43 round seeds and only 2 wrinkled. Does that single plant refute the coin-toss rule?
cards.back: Not by itself. Single plants scatter widely; a ratio should be estimated from the sum of many observations. Summed, the seeds gave 2.96 to 1. The plant is unusual, though.
cards.quote: Mendel held that a ratio should be estimated from the sum of many observations, since one plant is a small sample

cards.front: A family of 45 seeds from a selfed pea hybrid has about a 3 in 10,000 chance of 2 or fewer wrinkled seeds. If 253 such families were scored, what is the chance at least one came out that lopsided?
cards.back: 1 - (1 - 0.0003)^253 = about 0.07, so about 7 percent. Only a rough guide, since family sizes varied.
cards.quote: If all 253 of his hybrids had borne 45 seeds, the chance that at least one came out this lopsided would be about 7 percent.

cards.front: Why is a round pea of unknown genotype test-crossed to an rr plant?
cards.back: The rr tester gives only r, so each seed's phenotype reports which allele came from the unknown plant: RR x rr gives all round; Rr x rr gives 1/2 round : 1/2 wrinkled.
cards.quote: The rr tester can give only r, so each seed's phenotype reports which allele came from the unknown plant
cards.section: The test cross: reading a genotype you cannot see

cards.front: A round pea is test-crossed to rr and one seed comes out wrinkled. What is the round parent's genotype, and why?
cards.back: Rr: it carries r. The wrinkled seed is rr, the tester gave only one r, so the round parent gave the other (barring stray pollen).
cards.quote: A wrinkled seed is rr, the tester gave only one r, so the round parent gave the other.
cards.section: The test cross: reading a genotype you cannot see

cards.front: A round pea is test-crossed to rr and ten seeds are all round. If the plant were Rr, what is the chance of this result, and what does that number not tell you?
cards.back: (1/2)^10 = about 1 in 1,000. It is the chance of the result if the plant is Rr, not the chance that the plant is Rr: strong evidence for RR, not proof.
cards.quote: That is the chance of the result if the plant is Rr, not the chance that the plant is Rr.
cards.section: The test cross: reading a genotype you cannot see

cards.front: A double-hybrid round yellow pea (RrYy) was test-crossed to wrinkled green, once as seed parent and once as pollen parent. Both crosses gave four seed classes near 1:1:1:1. What does this show?
cards.back: The hybrid's eggs and its pollen each carried the four allele combinations (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in about equal numbers: shape and colour assort independently in both sexes.
cards.quote: Both are close to 1:1:1:1, so the hybrid's eggs and its pollen each carried the four allele combinations in about equal numbers.
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: What gamete types does an RrYy pea make, and in what proportions, if the loci assort independently?
cards.back: Four types, RY, Ry, rY and ry, at 1/4 each. The 16 equally likely unions sort into 9:3:3:1.
cards.quote: an RrYy plant makes four gamete types, RY, Ry, rY and ry, at 1/4 each
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: Selfed RrYy peas (round R and yellow Y dominant, loci independent) gave 556 seeds. How many wrinkled green seeds are expected?
cards.back: Wrinkled green = 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16. 556 / 16 = 34.75 expected (Mendel saw 32).
cards.quote: Wrinkled and green: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: A selfed RrYy pea cross gave 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green seeds. Compute the round : wrinkled ratio. What does it check?
cards.back: Round 315 + 108 = 423; wrinkled 101 + 32 = 133; 423 / 133 = 3.18 to 1. Seed shape alone still segregates near 3:1.
cards.quote: Two checks. Each character alone segregates near 3:1: round 315 + 108 = 423 to wrinkled 101 + 32 = 133 is 3.18 to 1
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: Selfed RrYy peas gave 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green. Without the 9:3:3:1 table, test whether colour affects the odds on shape.
cards.back: Fraction round among yellow = 315 / 416 = 0.757; among green = 108 / 140 = 0.771. Both near 3/4, so knowing colour does not change the odds on shape.
cards.why: Independence means the conditional chance equals the overall chance, the product rule from the other side.
cards.quote: knowing a seed's colour does not change the odds on its shape
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: Law of independent assortment: alleles at one locus enter gametes {{c1::independently}} of alleles at another.
cards.quote: This is the law of independent assortment: alleles at one locus enter gametes independently of alleles at another.
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: For which pairs of genes does independent assortment hold?
cards.back: Only for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on one. Pea seed shape and colour fit, but not every pair does.
cards.quote: Separate coins hold only for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on one

cards.front: A pea double hybrid got R with Y from one parent and r with y from the other. If shape and colour alleles usually, but not always, went into a gamete together, what would its test cross to wrinkled green show?
cards.back: Four classes, but unequal: round yellow and wrinkled green (the inherited combinations) clearly outnumber round green and wrinkled yellow.
cards.why: Fully joined would give only two classes; fully separate, four equal ones. This points to linkage.
cards.quote: Round yellow and wrinkled green, the combinations the hybrid inherited, would clearly outnumber round green and wrinkled yellow.
cards.section: Two characters: what the film left out

cards.front: Among round yellow seeds from a selfed RrYy pea (loci independent), what fraction should grow into plants that breed true for both shape and colour?
cards.back: Round seeds are 1/3 RR; yellow seeds are 1/3 YY. Independent loci: 1/3 x 1/3 = 1/9 are RRYY.
cards.why: Combines the F3 test (1 RR : 2 Rr among round) with the product rule for independent genes.
cards.quote: So one round plant in three should breed true, and two in three should give round and wrinkled seeds again.

cards.front: A tall purple pea (T tall, P purple, both dominant) is of unknown genotype. Design one cross that finds its genotype at both loci and tests independent assortment.
cards.back: Test-cross it to a true-breeding short white line (ttpp). Each offspring reads one gamete. TTPP: all tall purple. TtPP: tall and short 1:1. TTPp: purple and white 1:1. TtPp: four classes 1:1:1:1 if independent.
cards.quote: Test-cross it to a true-breeding short, white line (ttpp).

cards.front: A tall purple pea crossed to ttpp gives tall purple and short purple offspring at 1:1, and no white ones among many offspring. What is its genotype?
cards.back: TtPP. Short offspring show it carries t; no white offspring among many suggests it carries no p.
cards.quote: TtPP gives all purple, tall and short at 1:1.

cards.front: In a test cross where a class is expected at 1/4, what is the chance that the class is missing by chance among 20 offspring?
cards.back: (3/4)^20 = about 0.003. So with 20 or more offspring, an absent class is good evidence the allele is absent.
cards.quote: A class expected at 1/4 is missing by chance with probability (3/4)^n, about 0.003 for 20 offspring.

cards.front: What did Mendel not know about the basis of his 'elements'?
cards.back: He inferred them from counts and placed them in reproductive cells, but did not know of chromosomes or meiosis, which explain his laws.
cards.quote: He did not know of chromosomes or meiosis, which explain his laws

cards.front: Whose 1900 reports of crosses led to Mendel's pea paper being taken up?
cards.back: Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns, whose crosses followed his rules (Correns credited Mendel; de Vries's note did not; Tschermak's role is disputed).
cards.quote: not taken up until Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns reported crosses that followed his rules in 1900

cards.front: Is it true that each of Mendel's seven pea characters lies on a different one of the pea's seven chromosomes?
cards.back: No. Several lie on the same chromosome, and seed shape (R) and pod colour (Gp) are weakly linked.
cards.quote: It is false: several lie on the same chromosome, and seed shape (R) and pod colour (Gp) are weakly linked.
cards.section: Two later stories that need correcting
